Trying to Conceive

GnRH: hormone signals, testing and fertility treatment

Updated: November 8, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH, helps the brain coordinate reproductive function. The name also appears in discussions about puberty tests, fertility pumps and medicines that suppress hormones. These uses have different purposes. Understanding which signal or treatment your clinician means can help you ask useful questions without treating every missed period or fertility problem as a GnRH deficiency.

Where GnRH fits in the hormone pathway

Specialized nerve cells in the hypothalamus produce GnRH. Small blood vessels carry it to the anterior pituitary, which releases luteinizing hormone, LH, and follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH. These then act on the ovaries or testes. Together, the signals support egg development and ovulation, sperm production and the production of reproductive hormones.

GnRH is also called luteinizing-hormone-releasing hormone, LHRH, or luliberin. These names do not mean that it controls only LH. Gonadorelin is a manufactured version used in selected medical settings; a medicine name on a prescription should still be checked for the exact preparation and purpose.

Why the pattern of release matters

The hypothalamus normally sends GnRH in pulses. This pattern helps stimulate the pituitary rather than providing an unchanging hormone signal. Reproductive hormones feed back to the brain and pituitary, and the balance changes with development and across the menstrual cycle. Around ovulation, the feedback system permits the LH surge that helps release an egg.

A pulsatile gonadorelin treatment tries to replace a missing pattern of stimulation. Longer-acting GnRH agonist treatment can instead reduce the pituitary response after an initial stimulation. These opposite treatment effects are one reason that a pump, a diagnostic injection and an IVF suppression medicine must not be substituted for one another.

Symptoms need an assessment of the whole pathway

Reduced central hormone signalling can be associated with absent or delayed puberty, absent periods or impaired fertility. Some causes are present from birth; others develop later. However, similar symptoms can arise from problems in the ovaries or testes, thyroid disease, raised prolactin or other conditions. Symptoms alone cannot identify where the problem starts.

For absent periods, assessment usually begins with the history, examination and exclusion of pregnancy, followed by appropriate hormone tests. FSH, LH and sex-hormone results are interpreted together with the clinical circumstances. An apparently ordinary result on one laboratory report does not establish that the entire reproductive system is functioning normally.

What a GnRH stimulation test asks

A stimulation test examines the pituitary response after a medicine is given. It measures downstream hormones, usually LH and FSH, rather than simply counting the brain’s natural GnRH pulses. It may help investigate selected puberty disorders or suspected pituitary hormone problems. It is not a universal fertility test, and a normal response does not prove that conception will occur.

Testing is selected according to the question. The Endocrine Society’s 2026 guidance on central precocious puberty suggests starting with a sensitive baseline LH test when evaluation is indicated, rather than a stimulation test for every child. Further stimulation testing may be useful when clinical suspicion remains despite a low baseline result. The child’s development and rate of change matter alongside the numbers.

What to expect at the test appointment

A nurse or doctor explains the procedure and usually places a small cannula in a vein, allowing blood samples to be taken without a new needle each time. A baseline sample is followed by the stimulating medicine and timed samples. Some protocols use gonadorelin; others use a GnRH agonist. The route, sampling times and total visit length depend on the local protocol.

Follow the appointment instructions about eating, drinking and medicines. Some units allow normal meals for an isolated GnRH test, while a combined test may have different preparation. Bring the medicine list and disclose previous reactions, pituitary conditions, possible pregnancy or breastfeeding. The UK diagnostic product should not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding and is not recommended with a pituitary adenoma. Do not independently stop prescribed medicines to prepare.

A result has limits

The response must be interpreted using the laboratory’s method, age, pubertal stage and relevant hormone treatment. A single gonadorelin injection cannot by itself establish why a response is low or precisely locate every problem between the hypothalamus and pituitary. Clinicians may combine the result with other tests, imaging or follow-up rather than assign a diagnosis from one cutoff.

For delayed puberty, distinguishing a later normal start from lasting hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can be difficult. The 2025 Australasian pediatric testing handbook notes limited evidence for making that distinction with a GnRH stimulation test alone. Ask what the result changes now, what remains uncertain and when growth or pubertal progress should be reassessed.

When pulsatile treatment may help ovulation

Pulsatile GnRH can be considered for selected people whose lack of ovulation reflects inadequate hypothalamic signalling and whose pituitary can respond. It does not treat every cause of infertility. Before choosing it, the team needs a complete fertility assessment, including other factors that could prevent pregnancy, and a plan for monitoring the response.

In functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, nutritional shortfalls, excessive exercise relative to intake, illness or psychological stress may contribute. Addressing the underlying problem and restoring adequate energy availability are important parts of care. The Endocrine Society suggests pulsatile GnRH for suitable patients seeking pregnancy when available, after a complete workup; this recommendation is not an instruction to bypass recovery or start hormones without specialist assessment.

A pump needs a complete treatment service

A prescribed pump delivers small intermittent doses under a specialist plan. The clinic sets the medicine, delivery system, monitoring and any support after ovulation. An old description of a pulse every 90 minutes is not a schedule to program yourself. Nor can ovulation, pregnancy or completion of treatment be promised within two or three weeks.

Access requires both the medicine and a compatible delivery system. In a December 2024 notice hosted by the French regulator, Ferring reported that manufacture of the LutrePulse system had stopped and warned of a prolonged interruption. An old product page is therefore not proof that a clinic can supply the full treatment now. Ask about current local access, alternatives, training, costs and the plan if delivery stops.

Treatment goals in men and IVF are different

Selected men with deficient hypothalamic signalling may receive pulsatile GnRH to support sperm production. Gonadotropin treatment using hCG and FSH is another specialist approach. The European Association of Urology notes that GnRH treatment has administration and cost disadvantages and has not shown an advantage over gonadotropins for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. No sperm in a sample does not automatically mean a pump is appropriate; obstruction and testicular causes require different evaluation.

During IVF, an agonist such as buserelin may suppress an early LH surge while other medicines stimulate follicles. An antagonist such as cetrorelix blocks the receptor without the initial stimulatory effect. Some agonist products also have roles in endometriosis or fibroid care. These are distinct from replacing deficient GnRH pulses; the established BeMama guide to GnRH agonists covers their medicine-specific uses and precautions.

Monitoring and symptoms that should not wait

During fertility treatment, attend the planned reviews and report problems with the injection site or delivery system. Pulsatile treatment still needs discussion of ovarian hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancy risks. Contact the fertility team promptly for increasing abdominal pain or swelling, vomiting or reduced urine; seek urgent assessment if the team cannot be reached. These symptoms should not be managed by changing the pump setting yourself.

Tell staff immediately if you feel unwell during a test or injection. Severe breathing difficulty, throat swelling or collapse requires emergency help. A sudden severe headache or new visual disturbance also needs emergency assessment, especially with a known pituitary problem. Bring the exact medicine details, and ask the team for written instructions about routine side effects, missed delivery and who will explain the results.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Separate normal hormone physiology, diagnostic stimulation, pulsatile replacement and suppression medicines.

Interpret testing within a specialist assessment; age, laboratory methods and clinical development affect meaning.

Verify the diagnosis, treatment goal, delivery-system availability and monitoring before considering a pump.

How BeMama can help

Bring your test request or exact medicine name to the appointment. Ask what question it addresses, what the result can change and how follow-up will work.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for severe breathing problems, throat swelling, collapse, sudden severe headache or new visual disturbance. Increasing abdominal symptoms, vomiting or reduced urine during fertility treatment need prompt assessment. Do not improvise medicine changes or pump settings.

Evidence notes updated: November 8, 2026

Key takeaways

  • GnRH connects hypothalamic signals to pituitary LH and FSH release.
  • A diagnostic injection, pulsatile replacement and hormone suppression have different purposes.
  • Stimulation results require clinical context and do not settle every puberty or fertility question.
  • Pulsatile treatment is a specialist option for selected causes, with access and monitoring requirements.
  • Do not alter medicines or pump settings yourself; concerning treatment symptoms need timely care.

Frequently asked questions

Is GnRH the same as LH or FSH?

No. GnRH comes from the hypothalamus and signals the pituitary to release LH and FSH. Those hormones then act on the ovaries or testes. A problem at different points in this pathway can lead to similar symptoms.

Is gonadorelin only an intravenous medicine?

No. The route depends on the product and purpose. Diagnostic preparations may be given into a vein or under the skin, while selected pulsatile systems use subcutaneous delivery. Follow the exact prescription and clinic instructions.

Will I need repeated injections during a stimulation test?

Many protocols use one stimulating dose followed by timed blood samples through a cannula. The number of samples and the medicine vary. Ask the unit for its own procedure rather than relying on a general online timetable.

Can the test prove that delayed puberty is permanent?

Not by itself. There can be overlap between a later normal start and persistent hormone deficiency. The clinician interprets the response alongside growth, pubertal development, other investigations and sometimes observation over time.

Does a GnRH pump help everyone who is not ovulating?

No. It is considered for selected hypothalamic causes after a full assessment. Primary ovarian problems, other hormone disorders and additional fertility factors may need different treatment. The pituitary also needs to be able to respond.

Is LutrePulse routinely available?

Do not assume so. A manufacturer notice documented a prolonged delivery-system interruption. Availability differs by place and time, and a medicine listing does not confirm access to a compatible pump. Ask the treating center to verify the complete service.

Why can a GnRH-related medicine suppress hormones?

The effect depends on the medicine and pattern of exposure. Ongoing agonist treatment can suppress pituitary signalling after an initial stimulation; antagonists block the receptor directly. Pulsatile gonadorelin replacement has a different goal.

Should I stop hormones before the test?

Some medicines can affect interpretation, so give the unit a complete list and ask for written preparation instructions. Do not stop contraception, hormone replacement or another prescription yourself. Tell the team if pregnancy is possible or you are breastfeeding.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
